tagalog_lakapati.name: Grant the rice-fields their increase

term.value: Lakapati, pakanin mo yaring alipin mo

tagalog_lakapati.notes: Invoked at sowing to make the cultivated land bear; the planter raised a child over the field with the prayer 'Lakapati, feed thy servant, suffer him not to hunger.'

sources.reference: Pedro de San Buenaventura, Vocabulario de la lengua tagala (1613)
Boxer Codex (c. 1590)

tagalog_lakapati.name: Give the fish of river and sea
tagalog_lakapati.notes: Besought for water for the fields and for a good catch when the people went fishing in the sea.

sources.reference: Boxer Codex (c. 1590)

tagalog_mapulon.name: Turn the round of the seasons
tagalog_mapulon.notes: As the Tagalog god of the seasons he governs the alternation of the agricultural year, the turning that brings sowing and harvest.

sources.reference: F. Landa Jocano, Outline of Philippine Mythology (1969)

tagalog_idianale.name: Prosper labour and good works
tagalog_idianale.notes: Goddess of labour and good deeds; the people called on her to make their work succeed, and she is reckoned a patroness of husbandry.

sources.reference: F. Landa Jocano, Outline of Philippine Mythology (1969)

tagalog_hangin.name: Drive and still the winds
tagalog_hangin.notes: God of the wind among the seven children of Bathala; he rouses and calms the winds, often acting together with the storm-goddess Anitun Tabu and his brother Kidlat.

sources.reference: Oriental Mindoro tradition of Bathala's children, in Philippine folklore collections

tagalog_kidlat.name: Hurl the lightning
tagalog_kidlat.notes: God of the lightning among the children of Bathala; his flashes accompany the storms of Anitun Tabu and the winds of his brother Hangin.

sources.reference: Oriental Mindoro tradition of Bathala's children, in Philippine folklore collections

tamil_valli.name: Guard the millet field of the hill-people
tamil_valli.notes: As a girl of the Kuṟavar she kept watch over the tiṉai (millet) clearing on Vaḷḷimalai, driving off the parrots; there Murukaṉ wooed her in the guise of a hill hunter.

sources.reference: Kacciyappa Civāccāriyar, Kanta Purāṇam (14th c.), Vaḷḷi-tirumaṇam

tamil_valli.name: Embody the power of divine longing (icchā-śakti)
tamil_valli.notes: Beside Devasēṉā (kriyā-śakti), Vaḷḷi personifies icchā-śakti, the will or yearning of the soul drawing it to god; her winning by Murukaṉ figures the union of the human soul with the divine.

sources.reference: Kamil Zvelebil, Tiru Murugan (1981)

tahitian_ruahatu.name: Avenge the broken rāhui
tahitian_ruahatu.notes: When two fishermen tangled their hooks in his hair as he slept among the coral, the sea-god rose in wrath and resolved to drown all the land of Ra'iātea, sparing only those who fled to the islet of refuge.

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (Bishop Museum, 1928)

taino_marohu.name: Bring cloudless skies and the sun
taino_marohu.notes: The fair-weather twin who clears the sky and brings the sun, balancing his brother Boinayel the rain-bringer; the two stood as bound stone zemis in the cave of their mother Iguanaboina.

sources.reference: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)

tagalog_tala.name: Carry the orbs of starlight that guide night-travellers
tagalog_tala.notes: As goddess of the morning and evening star (Venus) Tala leads the stars out at dusk and draws them in at dawn, bearing light-orbs to guide those abroad in the dark.

sources.reference: Tagalog star-lore; F. Landa Jocano, Outline of Philippine Mythology (1969)

sources.reference: Kanta Purāṇam, Vaḷḷi-tirumaṇam

tagalog_lakapati.name: Planting-rite of Lakapati (maganito)
tagalog_lakapati.notes: At the start of planting the farmer lifted a child over the cultivated field and chanted 'Lakapati, feed this thy servant, suffer him not to hunger'; food and words were offered to the androgyne deity, asking water for the fields and fish from the sea.

sources.reference: Pedro de San Buenaventura, Vocabulario de la lengua tagala (1613)
Boxer Codex (c. 1590)

tahitian_oro.name: Cult of 'Oro at Taputapuātea
tahitian_oro.notes: At the great marae Taputapuātea 'Oro received offerings alternating human victims (skulls broken with a casse-tête) and fish laid before his to'o-image; intertribal alliances of the 'arioi convened there, and the feathered to'o was carried to battle.

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (Bishop Museum, 1928)
William Ellis, Polynesian Researches (1829)

tahitian_ruahatu.name: Cult of the sea-god and the rāhui
tahitian_ruahatu.notes: Ruahatu's deluge-myth was recited by the priests of Ra'iātea (recorded from Pa'ora'i and Vai'au by Orsmond) as the sanction behind the rāhui — the sacred prohibition on fishing certain grounds; to violate his repose was to invite the drowning of the land.

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (Bishop Museum, 1928)

tahitian_roo.name: First-fruits offering to Ro'o
tahitian_roo.notes: As the Society-Islands Rongo/Lono, god of the soil's produce and the weather, Ro'o received the first breadfruit and harvest offerings; he is also the herald and orator of the gods, especially of Tāne.

sources.reference: William Ellis, Polynesian Researches (1829)
Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (Bishop Museum, 1928)

thracian_derzelas.name: Darzaleia of Odessos
thracian_derzelas.notes: Quinquennial games (the Darzaleia) with athletic and musical contests were held in honour of the Great God at Odessos; the emperor Gordian III is thought to have attended in 238 CE, and the god's cult-statue and temple appear on the city's coinage.

sources.reference: Coinage and inscriptions of Odessos (Varna)

thracian_kendrisos.name: Kendreiseia (Pythian games) of Philippopolis
thracian_kendrisos.notes: As city-patron of Philippopolis, Apollo Kendrisos had his temple and statue struck on the civic coinage and the Kendreiseia (joined under Caracalla/Elagabalus to Pythian games) celebrated in his honour; his image remained that of the Thracian Horseman though he bore Apollo's name.

sources.reference: Coinage of Philippopolis; altar of Bithys to Apollo Kendrisos (IGBulgaria III 918)

thracian_gebeleizis.name: Arrow-shooting at the storm-sky
thracian_gebeleizis.notes: Herodotus reports that the Getae, when it thundered and lightened, shot arrows up at the sky and uttered threats, acknowledging no god but their own (Gebeleizis / Zalmoxis); they sent a messenger every five years by tossing him onto upright spears.

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 4.94

thracian_kandaon.name: Sacrifice by the sword of Kandaon
thracian_kandaon.notes: Lycophron names a human sacrifice performed with the 'three-fathered sword of Kandaon', the war-god worshipped by the Crestonian Thracians and glossed by the scholiasts now as Ares, now as Orion.

sources.reference: Lycophron, Alexandra 328 with scholia

taino_maquetaurie_guayaba.name: Cult of the dead in Coaybay
taino_maquetaurie_guayaba.notes: The op'a/opias (souls of the dead) dwelt in Coaybay under Maquetaurie Guayaba, hiding by day and emerging at night to feed on guava; Pané records the test for telling a living person from an op'a (the dead lack a navel) and the dog-zemi Opiyelguabirán who chased back fleeing souls.

sources.reference: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)

taino_guabancex.name: Storm-aversion offerings to Guabancex
taino_guabancex.notes: The cacical lords sent for and made offerings to the spiral-armed zemi of Guabancex, lady of the winds, when storms threatened; with her herald Guataubá (thunder) and Coatrisquie (the floods) she loosed the hurricane.

sources.reference: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)

tagalog_tala.name: Veneration of the morning and evening star
tagalog_tala.cadence: at the rising of Venus, dawn and dusk
tagalog_tala.notes: Plasencia records that the early Tagalogs worshipped certain stars, naming Tala the morning star, with Balatik (Orion) and Mapulon (the Pleiades); the planet Venus was watched and adored as a guide for night travel and the agricultural calendar.

sources.reference: Pedro de San Buenaventura, Vocabulario de la lengua tagala (1613)
Juan de Plasencia, Relación de las Costumbres de los Tagalos (1589)

attributes.name: The to'o, a sennit-wrapped wooden core feathered red and yellow
attributes.notes: 'Oro was not shown in human form but as a to'o: a length of aito (ironwood) bound in plaited coconut-fibre sennit with red and yellow feathers worked between the layers, the feathers being the body of the god.

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (Bishop Museum, 1928)
William Ellis, Polynesian Researches (1829)

sacredPlants.name: Aito / toa (ironwood, Casuarina) of the to'o core

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (Bishop Museum, 1928)

attributes.name: The woman seated in the full moon
attributes.notes: Hina is the figure seen in the moon, having stepped there from her brother Ru's canoe; beside her stands her banyan and the implements of tapa-making.

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (Bishop Museum, 1928)

sacredPlants.name: The banyan tree (ora) in the moon

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (Bishop Museum, 1928)

attributes.name: Man with the body/tail of a swordfish (a'u)
attributes.notes: Ruahatu's form is that of a man joined to a swordfish; he reposes among the coral groves of the deep, his long hair flowing, where the fishermen's hooks caught.

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (Bishop Museum, 1928)
Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (Bishop Museum, 1928)

attributes.name: Red and yellow feathers of the war-god
attributes.notes: Like 'Oro, the war-god Tū was embodied in feathered images; red and yellow feathers, the colour of warfare and of the gods, were placed within the sennit wrappings of his image.

sources.reference: William Ellis, Polynesian Researches (1829)

attributes.name: Reckoned by the bat, emblem of the wandering dead
attributes.notes: His emblem is the bat; the souls (op'a) that emerge by night to eat guava were imagined as bats, linking the lord of Coaybay to both fruit and the flitting dead.

sources.reference: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)
Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)
Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)

attributes.name: Weeping rain-zemi (llora-lluvias)
attributes.notes: The stone zemi of Boinayel was carved with lines trailing down the face like tears, marking him as a 'rain-crier' whose weeping is the rain that waters the cassava fields; he and Márohu stood, hands bound and seeming to sweat, in the cave of Iguanaboina.

sources.reference: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)

attributes.name: The mottled grey serpent that coils the rain into cloud
attributes.notes: Iguanaboina is figured as a humanised serpent or lizard (her name joining iguana with boina, the dark snake); she gathers the rain of the tropical sky into thickening cloud, and in her cave dwell her twin sons Boinayel and Márohu.

sources.reference: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)
Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)

attributes.name: The one-eyed moon-goddess
attributes.notes: In the Pampangan tradition Mayari lost an eye in her duel with her brother Apolaki, fought with bamboo war-clubs after Bathala's death; her dimmed light explains why the moon shines cooler and fainter than the sun.

sources.reference: Pampangan oral tradition; F. Landa Jocano, Outline of Philippine Mythology (1969)
Sangam corpus; Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai

sacredAnimals.name: White stallion of the night patrol

sources.reference: South Indian folk tradition; votive terracotta horses of Aiyaṉār shrines

sacredAnimals.name: The hind / deer of the huntress

sources.reference: Iconography of Bendis assimilated to Artemis; votive reliefs from the Bendideion, Piraeus

attributes.name: Woman wringing a flood from her long hair
attributes.notes: Nang Thorani is shown as a maiden wringing torrents of water from her hair — the merit-water the Buddha had poured out over many lives — which sweeps away the army of Māra; she stands or kneels below the earth-touching Buddha as his witness.

sources.reference: Paṭhamasambodhi (life of the Buddha); Thai temple murals

attributes.name: Glowing fireballs rising from the Mekong
attributes.notes: At the end of the rains-retreat ( Wan Ɔ̄k Phansā) the nak is said to breathe up reddish fireballs (bang fai phaya nak) from the river in homage to the Buddha's descent from Tāvatiṃsa; temple stairways are flanked by his multi-headed serpent balustrades.

sources.reference: Lao-Thai Mekong folklore; Bang Fai Phaya Nak tradition, Nong Khai

attributes.name: The artisan's adze (to'i) and the finished heavens
attributes.notes: As first of the great gods shaped by the artisans and patron of canoe-builders and woodworkers, Tāne is figured by the polished basalt adze; he it was who finished the sky, fixing the stars and hanging the sun and moon.

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (Bishop Museum, 1928)
William Ellis, Polynesian Researches (1829)

attributes.name: The fishhook that hauled up the land
attributes.notes: Māui is figured by his sacred fishhook, with which he drew islands up from the sea-floor, and by the noose/grip with which he snared the sun's rays to slow its course; in Tahiti he was remembered as a priest and prophet afterward deified.

sources.reference: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (Bishop Museum, 1928)
William Ellis, Polynesian Researches (1829)

attributes.name: Three-pointed stone (trigonolito) buried in the conuco
attributes.notes: Yúcahu was embodied in three-pointed stones (trigonolitos), often bearing a face on one point, which were set in the cassava-mounds of the conuco to make the yuca grow; he is the supreme spirit, lord of cassava and the sea.

sources.reference: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)
Antillean trigonolito sculpture, c. 1000-1500 CE
Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)

attributes.name: Frog-legged figure in the birthing posture
attributes.notes: Atabey, mother of the waters and of Yúcahu, is rendered in Taíno art as a squatting female with frog-like legs in the attitude of childbirth, hands to her face, expressing her power over fertility and birth; the coquí frog was held sacred to her.

sources.reference: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)
Antillean cohoba and stone iconography of the mother-zemi
Antillean Taíno iconography of the mother-goddess

attributes.name: Bound stone zemi of fair weather in Iguanaboina's cave
attributes.notes: With his weeping twin Boinayel, Márohu stood as a small stone zemi with hands bound, seeming to sweat, in their mother's cave; when rain was wanted the Taíno visited the cave, and where Boinayel weeps the rain Márohu clears the sky.

sources.reference: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)

attributes.name: Bearer of light-orbs, the morning and evening star
attributes.notes: Tala is imagined carrying orbs of light to guide travellers in the dark; she is the planet Venus, leading the stars out at evening and gathering them in at dawn. A possible identification with the goddess Tārā is suggested by the Majapahit-era Golden Tara of Agusan.

sources.reference: Tagalog star-lore; F. Landa Jocano, Outline of Philippine Mythology (1969)

attributes.name: Herald's staff (kerykeion) and ram, as the Hermes of the Mysteries
attributes.notes: As the youthful attendant of the Great Gods, identified by the Greeks with Hermes, Kadmilos bore the herald's staff and was associated with the ram; in the Samothracian rite the child of the goddess was understood to be in some mystic sense also her consort.

sources.reference: Mythography of the Samothracian Mysteries; Acusilaus apud Strabo, Geography 10.3
